en: The *Piṇḍīkrama*,
composed by the master Nāgārjuna,
is the *Piṇḍīkrama*.
Homage to the Omniscient One!
[He is] liberated from the conduct of the three worlds, attained like space, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena—
pure, peaceful, secluded, consisting of supreme bliss, and accessible only to yogins.

I pay homage to the body of the Victors—difficult to comprehend, difficult to analyze, most beneficial to oneself and others, all-pervading, causeless, blissful, unequaled by any equal, and the singular form of non-conceptuality. (Pik 1)
Through the realization of the sixfold meaning of the glorious *Samāja-tantra*, I shall explain the *Piṇḍīkrama* (the Condensed Stage), which arises for the benefit of all sentient beings. (Pik 2)
Having clearly perceived those defects of the habitual tendencies of conceptual construction which delude the three worlds, the wise one should purify them by means of the yoga-tantra. (Pik 3)
Having renounced the five sensual pleasures, one should not afflict oneself with austerities;
rather, one should maintain awakening with ease, in accordance with the Yoga Tantras.
Therefore, established here in the vow and remaining forever undifferentiated from the practitioner, he should begin the practice of the vajra of body, speech, and mind. (Pik 5)
In great forest regions adorned with fruits, flowers, and the like,
or on a solitary mountain, one should accomplish the compendium of all siddhis.
Seated on a soft cushion, established in the sattvaparyaṅka posture, and abiding in the Dveṣavajra samādhi, one should contemplate the protection of the site. // Pik_7 //
Having emitted the ten wrathful deities, blazing and terrifying with their radiant flames,
they stand upon the sun arising from the syllable *HŪṂ*, positioned in the *pratyālīḍha* stance.

Having thus visualized [the deities] in sequence at the forefront of the circles of the ten directions, one should command Sumbha and drive him with a stake for the purpose of destroying all obstacles. (Pik 9)
Aṃ sumbha niḥsumbha hūṃ! Gr̥hṇa gr̥hṇa hūṃ! Gr̥hṇāpaya gr̥hṇāpaya hūṃ! Ānaya ho bhagavan vidyārāja hūṃ phaṭ!
Having thus drawn in the Vināyakas by means of this wrathful form, the wise one should pierce them all according to the ritual procedure through this application. (Pik 10)
One should visualize the great king Vajrāmṛta as the wedge of the host,
dark blue like the petal of a blue lotus, and surrounded by a garland of blazing flames.

One should visualize the lower portion from the region of the navel as having the form of a trident, and the upper portion as having the form of a wrathful deity with three faces and six arms. (Pik 12)
Beholding the hosts of obstructors below and reciting the mantra, one should firmly drive the vajra-stake into the bodies of those obstructors. (Pik 13)

Oṃ gha gha ghātaya ghātaya all evil ones phaṭ phaṭ! Kīlaya kīlaya all sins phaṭ phaṭ! Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ! O Vajrakīla, Vajradhara commands: nail down the body, speech, and mind-vajras of all obstructors! Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! One should visualize Sumbharāja with a vajra-mallet in his hand.
Having visualized the vajra-fire blazing forth in all directions,
one should indeed imagine the wicked and the malicious being burned here and there.
Having fixed the ten directions and having established the below and above, one should meditate upon the three worlds as being without intrinsic nature according to the ultimate truth.
In the absence of existence, there is no meditation; meditation is indeed not meditation.
Thus, an entity would not be an entity; no mental cultivation is perceived.
Having meditated on the moving and stationary world as empty by means of this verse,
the ground of gnosis is attained through this application of the ritual method.
Situated in the midst of the space element, one should visualize the wind mandala,
produced from the seed-syllables *dvi-hūṃ* and *yaṃ*, and joined with two vajras.
And one should also visualize a circle of fire above that,
produced from the seed-syllables *dvi-hūṃ* and *raṃ*, marked with two vajras.
One should also visualize a circle of water above that,
produced from the seed-syllables *dvi-hūṃ* and *vaṃ*, joined with two vajras.
And one should also visualize a small circle of the earth above that, produced from the seed-syllables *dvi-hūṃ* and *laṃ*, and endowed with two vajras. (Pik 29)
In the withdrawal of the four maṇḍalas, there is the maṇḍala of the vajra-ground; therein, one should visualize a gabled palace produced from the syllable *bhrūṃ*. (Pik 22)
It is square, with four gates, adorned with four archways, provided with four boundary lines, and beautified by eight pillars. // Pik_23 //
Adorned with necklaces and half-necklaces, and featuring jewels, diamonds, and crescent moons,
it is inlaid with vajra-gems at the joints of the door-frames and projections.
The great vajra pillar with a water-pot base, the bird-shaped pinnacle, adorned with bells and banners, and decorated with chowries and other ornaments. (Pik 25)
In the central mandala, one should meditate upon oneself joined with the mudrā,
having three faces and six arms, with a complexion like that of a sapphire.
Śrī Vairocana, Ratna, Amitābha, and Karmarāj are to be visualized in the directions starting from the east, each having three faces and six arms. (Pik 27)
The goddesses, Mōharati and the others, having three faces and six arms, should be arranged in order, beginning from the south-eastern direction. (Pik 28)
Likewise, Rūpavajrā and the others are situated in the four outer corners;
Sparśavajrā alone is joined with Vajrasattva.
On the front panel, one should place Maitreya and Kṣitigarbha;
the practitioner should place Vajrapāṇi and Khagarbha on the right side. (Pik 30)
Furthermore, one should place Lokeśa and Mañjughoṣa in the west,
and Sarvāvaraṇaviṣkambhin and Samantabhadra in the north.
Yamāntaka is at the eastern gate, Aparājita at the southern,
Hayagrīva at the western, and Amṛtakuṇḍalī at the northern.
Acala, Ṭakkirāja, and the mighty Nīladaṇḍa should be visualized in their respective places, beginning from the eastern corner. (Pik 33)
One should visualize the great wrathful king Sumbharāja below,
and likewise visualize Uṣṇīṣacakravartin above.
Having thus meditated upon the deities of the maṇḍala according to the ritual procedure through resolute conviction,
one should again cause them to enter into one's own body by means of the yoga of union.
Having thus reflected upon the Buddhas residing within the body-mandala according to their respective positions,
one should cause them to enter into suchness by means of the ultimate mandala.
One should destroy the approaching array and will thereby attain success most effectively;
the meaning of this is explained extensively and clearly in the *Vajramālā*.
The mirror-like [wisdom] belonging to the aggregate of form consists of the earth element, the eye faculty, and form as the fifth; it proceeds in conjunction with Krodha and Maitreya.
The aggregate of sensation is the water element, the faculty of hearing, and sound as the fifth; these proceed together with the two forms of anger.
Perception, discernment, fire, the nasal faculty,
and odor— these five proceed together with the two types of anger.
Formative activity (saṃskāra), the performance of rites, the wind element, the organ of taste, and the fifth, the sense of taste—these proceed together with the two types of anger. (Pik 41)
Above and below, conjoined with wrath, and appearing as the very nature [of reality],
the aggregate of consciousness arises, and consciousness itself is luminosity.
Nirvāṇa is called the universal void and the Dharmakāya;
for the purpose of providing firmness, one should recite this mantra.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the knowledge of emptiness.
This is indeed the ultimate maṇḍala, free from appearance and devoid of characteristics;
it is also named the ultimate truth, the abode of all Tathāgatas. (Pik 44)
The emergence from the state of luminosity is also demonstrated through the application of the mantra-form,
directed toward the visualization of the deity.
Situated in the center of the space element, one should visualize a solar disc;
above that, the practitioner of mantra should further visualize a lunar orb.
There, one should visualize an eight-petaled lotus of red color;
upon that lotus, one should further visualize the great mantra consisting of three syllables. (Pik 47)
One should visualize the mantra, the lotus, and likewise the sun as having entered the lunar disc;
one should meditate upon the lunar disc as being completely filled with the bodhicitta.
One should contemplate all that is stationary and all that is moving as being right there;
for the purpose of strengthening [the visualization], one should recite this mantra. (Pik 49)
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the essence of the *dharmadhātu*.
Having thus taken hold of the yoga, one should practice the subsequent yoga (*anuyoga*).
Furthermore, the yogi should contemplate the three syllables in the center of the moon. (Pik 50)
Then, having visualized the Primordial Lord (Ādinātha), who arises from three syllables and resembles a white kunda flower or the moon, one should commence the Atiyoga.
Through the entry into Akṣobhya, one should visualize Vajrasattva with three faces and six arms, blazing and radiant with the luster of sapphire. (Pik 52)
One should visualize a vajra, a wheel, and a lotus in the right hands;
one should visualize a bell, a jewel, and a sword in the left hands. (Pik 53)

Then, one who knows the divisions of the shoulders and other limbs should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) according to reality, through the placement of seed-syllables (*bīja*), beginning with Vairocana and ending with Sumbha. (Pik 54)
The mantra-knower should place the seed-syllable of Vairocana, the syllable Oṃ, white in color, upon the head as the intrinsic nature of the aggregate of form.

Having meditated on the syllable ĀḤ at the mouth as belonging to Amitābha and having the nature of the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha), red in color, one shall attain mastery over speech. Pik_56
The practitioner of mantra should place the syllable HŪṂ of Akṣobhya, which has the brilliant luster of lapis lazuli,
in the heart as the form of the aggregate of consciousness.
One should place the yellow-colored self-form of the Lord of Jewels at the navel, in the form of the aggregate of sensation, as the cause for the purification of sensation. (Pik 58)

The mantra-practitioner should, according to the reality of the Lord of Karma, place the syllable *hāḥ*, which is greenish in appearance, upon the two feet by virtue of its nature as the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). (Pik 59)
Through passion for delusion and so forth, the practitioner should cause earth and the other elements to enter;
these [elements] possess, respectively, hardness, fluidity, heat, and mobility. (Pik 60)
Having placed the syllable *thlīṃ* upon the eyes, one should visualize Kṣitigarbha;
having placed the syllable *oṃ* upon the ears, one should visualize Vajrapāṇi. (Pik 61)
One should place the syllable Oṃ on the nose and visualize Khagarbha;
having meditated on the syllable Oṃ on the tongue, one should contemplate Lokeśa. (Pik 62)
Having meditated on the syllable *hūṃ* in the mind, one should visualize Mañjughoṣa;
and having meditated on the syllable *oṃ* in the entire body, one should recollect Viṣkambhin.
One should visualize Maitreya residing in the head with the syllable *maiṃ*;
having meditated upon Bhadra on all sides, one should place him at all the joints.
Yamāntaka is to be visualized on the right arm, Aparājita on the left;
Hayagrīva is to be visualized in the mouth, and Amṛtakuṇḍalin on the vajra.
One should visualize Acala on the right side and Ṭakkirāja on the left;
and at the right knee, one should contemplate Nīladaṇḍa, who is exceedingly radiant.
One should visualize Mahābala on the left knee and Uṣṇīṣacakrin upon the head,
with Sumbharāja placed at the two ends of the feet.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the shoulders and other parts according to the rule, the mantra-practitioner,
having entered the body-maṇḍala, should commence the Great Yoga (mahāyoga).
One should contemplate a full moon disc situated in the center of the crown;
therein is the syllable Oṃ, white in appearance and radiating five-colored rays of light.
Then, having brought forth the goddess through the application of sovereign power,
one should contemplate various Locanās filling the entire expanse of space.
Then, having visualized the body-vajra, established filling the sky,
one should contemplate the Lord in its center, standing before oneself.
Then the mantra-practitioner, reciting two verses, should pray to the one who bears the thirty-two marks and is adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics. (Pik 72)
Bearing the body of a Buddha, glorious, and cultivated through the indivisibility of the three vajras,
may he today grant me the state of empowerment as a Body-Vajra-holder.
May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, who have cultivated the indivisibility of the three vajras,
grant me today the state of empowerment as a Vajra Body.
One should visualize [the deity] as eternal and joined with Locanā;
having caused him to enter, one should preside over him, fully endowed with the five aggregates.
May my body also become like that of all the Buddhas, filled with the five aggregates by way of the intrinsic nature of the Buddha-body.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra-body of all Tathāgatas.
One should contemplate the syllable ĀḤ, red in color, situated in the center of the lotus of the tongue;
and one should emanate the goddess named Pāṇḍarā together with her retinue, filling the expanse of space. (Pik 77)
Then the mantra-practitioner, having filled the sky with the speech-vajra established therein, should offer a prayer while reciting two verses. (Pik 78)
May the glorious Dharma, the path of speech, which is cultivated as the indivisible nature of the three vajras,
grant me today the state of empowerment of the Vajra of Speech.
May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, who are conceived as the indivisibility of the three vajras,
grant me today the state of empowerment, O Vajra of Speech!
Having visualized Pāṇḍarā, joined with her own Lord,
suddenly entering the tongue, one should begin the consecration of speech.
Just as the speech of Vajradharma is perfected in expression,
may my speech likewise become like that of a Dharma-holder.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the speech-vajra of all Tathāgatas.
Having placed a brilliantly shining lunar disc at his heart, the mantra-practitioner [should place] there the syllable HŪṂ, resembling sapphire and possessing five-colored rays of light. (Pik 83)
Then one should emanate the goddess Māmakī together with her retinue;
having likewise meditated upon the Mind-Vajra, one should supplicate it as before.
The glorious holder of the mind-vajra, who is meditated upon as the indivisibility of the three vajras,
may he today grant me the state of empowerment of the Mind-Vajra-holder.
May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, who are realized as the indivisibility of the three vajras,
grant me today the state of empowerment, O Vajra-Mind!
Having caused the mind-vajra, joined in union, to enter into the heart,
one should begin the empowerment of the mind through the entire array of Māmakī.
May my mind also become like that of the wise Guhyakendra Samantabhadra— like the mind of Vajradhara.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra-mind of all Tathāgatas.
Having thus presided over [the deities] individually according to the division of the three families, the wise one should again make them of universal nature by means of this mantra: Pik_89.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas.
Having thus empowered myself as being situated in the center of a lunar disc, one should contemplate the Samayasattva endowed with the six signs. (Pik 90)
One should visualize the subtle Jñānasattva situated in the center of the heart;
one should firmly place the syllable HŪṂ, known as the Samādhisattva, within that.
Having thus accomplished the great yoga consisting of the three beings,
the self-possessed one should begin the great sādhana by means of this ritual application.
Having obtained the large-eyed maiden, adorned with beauty and youth,
dark as the petal of a blue lotus, from the noble-souled washerman.
Having taken hold of one who is well-trained and devoted to the practitioner, one should meditate on the syllable Oṃ at her head and place the syllable Āḥ in her throat. (Pik 94)
Having meditated on the syllable *hūṃ* at the heart, *svā* at the navel, and *hā* at both feet,
[one should likewise visualize] Locanā, Māmakī, and Pāṇḍaravāsinī.
The mantra-practitioner should likewise place Tārā upon the elements beginning with earth;
one should visualize the goddesses Rūpavajrā and the others in that very same place. (Pik 96)
One should visualize their union with Kṣitigarbha and the others;
Vajravetālī is on the right arm and Aparājitā on the left.
And upon her face is Bhṛkuṭī, and on the secret part is Ekajaṭā;
furthermore, situated on the right side is the Tathāgatī Viśvavajrī.
One should visualize the Viśvaratnā mudrā on the left,
and likewise the Viśvapadmā Tathāgatī situated upon the right knee.
And on the left [shoulder] is Viśvakarman, while on the crown of the head is Gaganavajriṇī;
and the goddess Dharaṇīndharā is placed at the two ends of the feet.
Having thus consecrated her, the yogi should begin with the vajra and lotus;
the mantra-practitioner should indeed meditate upon the five-pronged vajra born from the syllable *hūṃ*.
Likewise, one should visualize the *praṇava* at its center;
in that same way, one should visualize an eight-petaled lotus by means of the syllable *ĀḤ*.
Then, surrounded by five rays of light, one should begin the practice. (Pik 102)
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the Vajra of the passion of all Tathāgatas.

One should cause [the consort] to move by means of the song of the syllable Hūṃ, while maintaining the pride of the Vajra-holder. At the very moment one's own bodhicitta arises, one should utter the mantra Phaṭ. (Pik 103)
At the end of the emission, the mantra-practitioner should again worship with the bodhicitta;
he should utter this mantra to the Buddhas residing in the ten directions. (Pik 104)

Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of worship of all Tathāgatas. Having produced myself—perfected from the syllables of my own mantra and empowered by the three vajras—in the center of a lotus, one then becomes Dveṣavajra. (Pik 105)
One should behold Akṣobhyavajrin, produced from the mantra *vajradhṛk*, the Lord who wears a crown of matted locks with Akṣobhya as his crest-ornament. (Pik 106)
One should visualize [the deity] resembling a rain-cloud over the earth, with a face that is black, red, and white, adorned with all ornaments, and possessing six arms. 107.
One should hold a vajra, a wheel, and a lotus in the right hands;
one should visualize a bell, a wish-fulfilling jewel, and a sword in his left hands. (Pik 108)
Having emerged from the heart and surveyed the ten directions,
he performed the entire miraculous power of a Buddha and set the wheel of Dharma in motion.
Having purified all sentient beings who were established in the state of the Vajra of Hatred,
he returns and sits down before the Lord of the Vajra.
Having caused him to enter, the mantra-practitioner should contemplate himself within the heart;
having transformed his former form, he stands in the state of Dveṣavajra.
Blazing with the luster of a sapphire, situated in the center of a solar mandala, the Hero is embraced by his own mudrā and adorned with all ornaments. (Pik 112)
Resplendent with three faces—fierce, peaceful, and of great passion—he, established in the samādhi of Hatred-Vajra, should emanate the entire maṇḍala. (Pik 113)
One should emanate the all-pervading Vairocana, produced from the *jinajig* mantra,
resembling the rays of the autumn moon and adorned with a crown of matted locks.
One should visualize [the deity] with white, red, and black faces, possessing six arms and a peaceful form,
holding a wheel, a vajra, and a white lotus in the right hands.
One should visualize a bell, a wish-fulfilling gem, and a sword in his left hands;
likewise, from his heart, beings established in the conduct of delusion emerge. (Pik 116)
Having purified [the site] and returned once more, he sits down again;
the wise one should emanate Ratnaketu, who is produced from the *ratnadhṛk* mantra. (Pik 117)
One should also visualize him wearing a mass of matted hair, gentle in appearance, with Akṣobhya as his crest-jewel, possessing faces that are yellow, black, and white, and having six arms. (Pik 118)
One should visualize a wish-fulfilling gem, a vajra, and a wheel in his right hands;
and a bell, a yellow lotus, and a sword in his left hands. (Pik 119)
Having likewise emerged from the heart, she purifies those situated in the state of ego (ahaṅkāra) and sits upon the jewel in the southern quarter.
One should emanate Amitavajrin, produced from the ĀROLIṄ mantra, possessing the luster of a ruby, serene, and with Akṣobhya as his crest-ornament. (Pik 121)
One should visualize the Lord as wearing a crown of matted locks, with faces that are red, black, and white, endowed with the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), and possessing six arms. (Pik 122)
Holding the lotus stalk together with the bell in the left hand, one should cause the lotus situated at the region of the heart to blossom with the right hand. (Pik 123)
In his two right hands are a vajra and a wheel, while in his two left hands are a jewel and a sword;
having purified the passionate one as before, she sits upon a lotus behind him.
The mantra-practitioner should emanate the Lord Amoghavajrin, created by the mantra of Prajñādhṛk, green in appearance and adorned with a crown of matted hair. (Pik 125)
One should visualize [the deity] with green, black, and white faces, six arms, and radiant with rays of light;
in the right hands, one should conceive of a sword, a double-vajra (viśvavajra), and a wheel.
Holding a bell in his left hand and likewise a green lotus and a jewel,
he returned after having purified those beings who spoke untruths.
Likewise, in the northern direction, he sits upon the Viśvavajra;
[therein reside] Hatred, Delusion, Passion, the Wish-fulfilling Gem, and the Samaya.
These five families indeed accomplish both desire and liberation;
from the mantra of Moharatī, one should emanate the goddess Locanā. (Pik 129)
One should visualize her as white, endowed with the sentiment of tranquility (śāntarasa), marked by Vairocana upon her head,
and possessing six arms with faces that are white, red, and black.
One should visualize a wheel or a vajra in the right hand, and likewise a white lotus;
in the left hand, one should likewise visualize a bell, a jewel, and also a sword.
Emerging from the heart and surveying the ten directions,
she of great compassion brings peace to the world afflicted by planetary spirits and diseases.
Having arrived, she sits in the eastern corner in the middle of the wheel.
From the mantra of Dveṣarati, one should emanate the goddess Māmakī,
who is dark like the petal of a blue lotus, with a beautiful face and a charming form.
And her faces are black, red, and white, with Akṣobhya as her crest-ornament.
In the right hands, one should hold a vajra, a wheel, a blue lotus, a red lotus, a bell, a jewel, and a sword. 135.
Having provided protection for those afflicted by the fear of great obstacles, she of great compassion departs and,
returning once more, sits down in the southwest.
From the mantra born of passion and delight, one should emanate Pāṇḍaravāsinī,
whose faces are red, black, and white, and who possesses the luster of a ruby.
One should visualize her with a mass of matted hair adorned with Amitābha, possessing six arms,
holding the stalk of a blue lotus together with a bell in her left hand.
One should awaken the red lotus situated at the heart with the right [hand],
and the vajra and wheel with both right hands, while the jewel and sword are on the left.
Holding it, she emerges, brings peace to the greatly afflicted,
and having returned, she sits indeed in the middle of the lotus in the northwest corner.
From the mantra of Vajrarati, one should emanate the beautiful Tārā, whose faces are green, black, and white, and whose radiance is like the leaf of the dūrvā grass. (Pik 141)
One should visualize her as having six arms and being crowned by Amoghasiddhi;
in her right hands are a crossed-vajra and a wheel, and in [her left] an azure lotus.
The practitioner should place the bell, the jewel, and likewise the sword in the left [hands];
having brought all sentient beings under control, he sits again upon the Viśvavajra seat.
Having emerged and come together, he sits in the abode of Śiva;
in the second enclosure, however, the yogin should emanate Rūpavajrā and the others.
In the southeast corner, one should emanate the goddess Rūpavajrā,
who is enchanting, white in color, with three faces and six arms, and who bears Śrī Vairocana upon her crown.
One should place the six-armed goddess Śabdavajrā in the southwest (nairṛtya), holding a mirror with two hands, like the remaining [goddess] Moharatī.
She is yellow in color, has three faces, and bears Ratnasaṃbhava upon her crown;
her two hands are occupied with a lute, and the rest [of her attributes] should be as those of Māmakī.
One should place the goddess Gandhavajrā in the position of wind; she has six arms, is red in color, possesses three faces, and wears the matted locks of Amitābha.
And one should place the six-armed goddess Rasavajrā in the northeast, her two primary hands occupied with a conch shell, while the remaining hands hold the [other attributes] of Pāṇḍaravāsinī.

She has three faces and is dark green in color; she wears a crown with the head of Dundubhisvara, holds a vessel of nectar in one hand, and in her remaining hands, she has the same appearance as Tārā.
One should contemplate Sparśavajrā, who embraces Vajrasattva and is situated in the center of the wheel, equal to him in her faces and other features.
On the third layer, on the eastern panel,
the observer of vows should create Maitreya and Kṣitigarbha, produced from the seed-syllables Maiṃ and Thlīṃ.
The mantra-practitioner should create Vajrapāṇi and Khagarbha, who have arisen from the syllable *praṇava*,
on the southern panel in their proper order.
One should emanate Lokeśvara Mañjughoṣaka, produced from the syllable Oṃ-Hūṃ, in the western direction; furthermore, one should emanate these two in the northern direction as well.

[The deities] are produced from the seed-syllables Oṃ and Saṃ, together with Vighnāntaka and Samantaka; they wear their own lords as crowns, and furthermore, they are equal [to them] in color and other attributes. (Pik 155)
In their arms and with their weapons, they are equal to their respective lords;
Maitreya alone, however, carries a *nāgapuṣpa* flower in his left hand.
Having purified these sense bases, they bestow the divine eye and other faculties;
then, returning to sentient beings, they indeed sit upon their thrones.
The mantra-practitioner should emanate Yamāntaka, who arises from the mantra of Yamāntakṛt, possessing faces that are black, red, and white, and who is dense with excellent male organs. (Pik 158)
Holding a staff, a wheel, and likewise a vajra in his right hands,
he holds a threatening gesture with a noose, a bell, and an axe at the region of his heart from the left.
Terrifying the terrible obstacles as well as Indra and the others together with their retinues,
he stands in the eastern direction, treading upon a lotus and sun disk.

The mantra-practitioner should emanate Aparājita, who brings an end to ignorance, who originates from the mantra, who has Ratnasambhava as his crest-jewel, who is white in color, and adorned with serpents.
With faces white, black, and red, a large belly, and three eyes;
formidable with terrifying fangs and agitated by a dense mass of sparks.
Holding a vajra, a staff, and a sword in his right hands,
he holds a threatening gesture with a noose, a bell, and an axe at his heart and in his left hands.
Terrifying the terrible obstacles with his right leg extended in the pratyālīḍha posture,
he stands in the southern direction, treading upon a lotus and sun disk.
The practitioner should emanate Hayagrīva, born from the mantra of Yamāntaka;
he resembles a ruby, has three eyes, and faces that are red, black, and white. (Pik 165)
With a formidable face and a large belly, wearing a crown of immeasurable light,
the hero stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, enveloped in a dense mass of sparks.
One should visualize a lotus, a sword, and a club in the right hands,
and a bell, a proud axe, and a noose in the left hands.
Having mounted a lotus-sun disk and surveyed the ten directions,
he causes all obstacles to tremble with fear and stands in the western direction.
One should emanate Amṛtakuṇḍalin, who arises from the mantra that destroys obstacles, who has Dundubhisvara as his crest-jewel, and who is dark like the petal of a blue lotus.
With faces blue, red, and white, and the appearance of a gaping maw, he has a large belly, three eyes, and is adorned with red flames. (Pik 170)
He holds a double-vajra, a curved knife, and a club in his right hands, while holding a noose with the threatening gesture, a bell, and an axe in his left hands. (Pik 171)
Having performed the terrifying of obstacles with the pratyālīḍha stance,
he mounts a lotus-sun and stands in the northern direction.
One should again emanate Acala, who is produced from the syllables of his own mantra,
possessing the luster of sapphire, having three eyes, and bearing the illustrious Vairocana upon his crown.
With a face made terrifying by fangs, with faces black, red, and white,
making a terrible sound of loud laughter, possessing a vast belly and great strength.
One should hold a sword, a vajra, and likewise a wheel in the right hands;
and also a threatening gesture, an axe, and a noose in the left hands. (Pik 178)
Having destroyed obstacles such as fevers and the like, he stands upon a lotus and sun disk in the position of fire (the southeast) with his right leg extended in the *pratyālīḍha* posture. (Pik 176)
The practitioner should emanate Ṭakkirāja, produced from the syllables of his own mantra—a hero with the luster of sapphire and bearing a crown of Ratnasambhava. (Pik 177)
With faces that are black, red, and white, possessing a large belly and a terrifying appearance,
he holds a vajra and the *hūṃkāra* mudrā with his two hands.
Holding a vajra and a sword in his two right hands, and a noose and a goad in his left,
he stands upon the sun in the *pratyālīḍha* posture in the southwest, the destroyer of obstacles.
The practitioner should emanate Nīladaṇḍa, produced from the syllables of his own mantra;
he resembles a dark blue cloud, has three eyes, and wears a crown of Amitābha.
Having faces that are blue, red, and white, with a large belly and a terrifying appearance, he holds a staff and a sword in his right hands. (Pik 181)
In the region of the heart, [he holds] a noose with the index finger, a lotus, and an axe on the left;
having struck away the fear of calamities, he stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture.
Having mounted a lotus and sun disc, he stands in the northwestern direction;
he is produced from the syllables of his own mantra and has the sound of a drum as his crest-ornament.

The practitioner of mantra should create one of great power, with the luster of a blue lotus petal, possessing three faces—black, red, and white—and three eyes, resounding with a terrifying roar. (Pik 184)
With all his limbs adorned by serpents, possessing a large belly and a terrifying appearance,
he holds a staff, a sword, and likewise a discus in his right hands.
In the region of his heart, he holds a noose with the index finger, a lotus, and an axe on the left;
he is the destroyer of the fears of the Ḍākinīs and others, standing in the pratyālīḍha posture.
Having mounted a lotus and sun disk, he stands in the northeastern direction;
one should emanate the Uṣṇīṣacakrin, produced from the syllables of his own mantra.
Dark as the sky, terrible, with Akṣobhya as his crest-jewel,
possessing faces that are black, red, and white, three-eyed, pot-bellied, and all-pervading.
Holding the uṣṇīṣa upon his head with his left and right hands,
he holds a vajra and a lotus with his two right hands, and a threatening gesture and a sword with the other [two].
Destroyer of all calamities, standing with his left leg extended and right knee raised,
he mounts a lotus-sun and abides in the station of Brahmā.
The practitioner should emanate Sumbharāja, produced from the syllables of his own mantra;
he is brilliantly radiant like space, possesses three eyes, and has faces that are black, red, and white.
Having a large belly and a formidable mouth, with Akṣobhya as his crest-ornament, he holds a vajra, a wheel, and likewise a jewel in his right hands. (Pik 192)
At the region of the heart, she holds a noose with her index finger, and to the left, a lotus and a sword;
[she also holds] all poisons such as *kālakūṭa*, both stationary and mobile.
Having slain all the Vināyakas and established peace everywhere,
and having fully accomplished his command, he stands in the pratyālīḍha posture;
mounting a lotus and sun disk, he remains beneath the earth.
Having abandoned the entire mandala consisting of the thirty-two deities,
and having become situated in the center of the wheel, one should then begin the subtle yoga.

One should contemplate a mustard seed at the tip of the nose; within that mustard seed, one should meditate upon the delightful state of gnosis, the secret fashioned by gnosis, which contains all that is moving and unmoving.
One should expand a stable jewel, but one should never expand an unstable one;
one should expand it with excellent clouds possessing a radiance equal to the flames of a Buddha.
One who subsists on alms should not recite [the mantra], nor should one be devoted to begging;
rather, one may enjoy all desired pleasures while reciting the mantra with unimpaired limbs.
Having recited [the mantra], one should emanate the vajra; at the conclusion, one should perform the withdrawal.
This is said to be the recitation of all the Buddhas from the perspective of ultimate reality. Thus it is said. (Pik 199)
Having also divided the subtle yoga-recitation into two according to one's preference,
the mantra-practitioner should then cause himself to enter into suchness.
The four goddesses situated in the mandala, not seeing their Lord there,
awaken Mahāsukha in this way with a set of four verses.
O Vajrasattva, Lord of the World, O Refuge of the realm of beings, protect me with your passion, wisdom, and great purpose!
Love me, O Father, Great and Supreme Kinsman of beings, if you wish for me to live, O Protector! Pik_202

O Vajra-body, supreme wheel beloved by many beings, you who perceive the welfare of the ultimate meaning of enlightenment and the purpose of the Buddhas—desire me with passion, O one whose vow is passion, if you wish for my protector to live! Pik_203 //

O Vajra Speech, you who are compassionate for the benefit of all and always engaged in performing deeds for the sake of the world— O Samantabhadra, practice of the Sugatas, grant me your desire if you wish, O Protector, that I may live!
O Vajra-Lover, supreme of commitments, you who act for the great benefit of others, the ornament of the lineage of the Perfectly Awakened Ones, and compassionate in equanimity;
desire me, a treasury of virtues and a source of many jewels, if you wish, O Lord, that I may live!
Having thus aroused the Protector through the proclamation of his truly existing qualities,
the Tathāgatas praise him as having the nature of Akṣobhya and the other [Buddhas].
O Akṣobhyavajra, great wisdom, Vajradhātu, great Buddha, triple mandala, supreme among the three vajras, speak the secret; homage be to you! Pik_207
Vairocana, great purity, vajra peace, great delight; teach the phenomena that are luminous by nature, O Vajra, homage be to you! Pik_208
O King of Jewels, profoundly deep, stainless as the space of the vajra of emptiness, pure by nature and untainted—speak the secret; homage be to you! Pik_209
O Vajrāmita, Great King, free from conceptual construction, wielder of the space-vajra;
O you who have attained the perfection of sovereignty, speak, O Vajra—homage be to you!
O Amoghavajra, perfectly awakened one, who fulfills all hopes;
O Vajrasattva, born of the nature of purity—homage be to you!
Then, having praised and gladdened the Buddhas, and having revealed the supreme secret wheel as it truly is,
the Lord alone remains in great bliss, having established that wheel within his own body-wheel.

Thus, the yogi who employs the four yogas, having thoroughly contemplated the world as containing the syllable *hūṃ* at its core, and having seen it, mutters the Vajrasattva of that existence; then, having arisen, he should conduct himself with that wisdom exactly as prescribed. (Pik 213)
When the mantra practitioner, focusing on meditative absorption, becomes emaciated in body,
he should contemplate this yoga which brings delight to body, speech, and mind.
Having stepped forward a distance of one span, one should visualize a mandala upon the head;
having visualized the syllable Oṃ located there, one should bring down the five nectars.
By means of this vajra-yoga, one becomes radiant in an instant;
one attains the well-being of body, speech, and mind—of this there is no doubt. // Pik_216 //
In this way, through practice, the mantra practitioner should purify and awaken [the elements] just as he should purify the heart and throat, and thereby gratify the Tathāgatas.
Having purified it with the syllable *hūṃ*, one should awaken it with the syllable *āḥ*;
one should cause it to blaze while pervaded by the *praṇava* (*oṃ*). This is the purification of food.
First, having visualized a conch at the throat,
one should imagine an eight-petaled lotus arising from the syllable Hrīḥ within it, with the syllable Hūṃ upon its pericarp.
One should visualize the great five-pronged vajra born from the syllable *hūṃ*;
at the tip of its central prong, one should contemplate the syllable *oṃ*, which purifies the throat. (Pik 220)
Having meditated upon Meghanāda in the heart, one should then radiate the three-pointed fire;
there, one should offer food as an oblation—this indeed is the internal fire sacrifice (adhyātmika-homa).
He should kindle the fire of Vāyu; he cooks that which belongs to Varuṇa;
it is the station of the Maheśvara-maṇḍala where the oblation moves.
Whatever food and drink there may be, all of that, by means of the Vāruṇa [mudrā], one should cause to enter the heart-lotus through the lotus of the mouth. (Pik 223)
Thereafter, by means of the yoga of union, one should visualize [the syllable] having reached the navel-lotus,
emerged from the anus-lotus, and extended as far as the end of the ashes.
There is neither old age nor disease, neither death nor poison and the like;
for him there is no untimely death, as this is the destroyer of all calamities. (Pik 225)
By churning the ocean of the *Samāja* with the excellent churning-stick of the *Śrīvajramālā*, that nectar of the limbs of accomplishment was obtained;
by means of it, may the entire world attain immortality. (Pik 226)
The Sadhana of the Piṇḍīkrama is completed.
The work of the venerable master Ācārya Śrī Nāgārjuna.
